strengths: Well-motivated problem: the paper identifies a genuine gap in TTA evaluation—conventional protocols assume unbounded processing time—building on Alfarra et al. (2024) and extending the space with two additional deployment archetypes (user-led latency decay, resource-led budgets) that prior work does not cover.

The framework is cleanly formalised. Each utility metric decomposes into interpretable factors (availability vs. served accuracy; accuracy vs. responsiveness and alignment; adapted vs. frozen accuracy), which turns 'rank instability' from an observation into an explanation. Terms like 'computational insolvency' and the three failure modes (availability collapse, accuracy erosion, unproductive overhead) are useful conceptual contributions.

Careful methodological treatment of prior work: Appendix B's critique of Alfarra et al.'s protocol (risk-free fallback, stepped ceiling penalties, forced idling) is detailed and the buffered single-model revision is well justified, including subtle implementation issues (BN running-buffer modes after freezing).

Substantial, well-organised empirical evidence: 7 methods, 16 temporal scenarios, 15 corruptions, 240 evaluations, with per-corruption decompositions in the appendix and complete per-batch logs promised in supplementary code—good reproducibility practices.

Honest and thorough limitations discussion (single architecture, dataset, episodic i.i.d. setting, method exclusions, hardware dependence), and the SHOT-IM frozen-phase resilience finding is a genuinely non-obvious result invisible to offline evaluation.
Presentation quality is high: figures (1–4) and tables directly support the claims, and the rank-correlation analysis quantifies how instability varies with corruption type and pressure level.
weaknesses: Single seed for all reported results. Many headline claims are about rankings and win counts (141/240, 41.2% loss rate, Spearman correlations as extreme as r_s = -0.74); without repeated seeds or significance analysis, the stability of these rank-based statistics is not established, particularly since TTA methods are known to be sensitive to stochastic ordering.

Narrow empirical scope: one backbone (ResNet-50), one dataset (ImageNet-C severity 5), one GPU. The paper's own discussion concedes that trade-offs differ across architectures and hardware, but the generality of 'rank instability is pervasive' rests on a single configuration; results on even one additional backbone or a non-episodic stream would substantially strengthen the central claim.

The headline finding has a partially predictable structure: gradient-based methods have 2.4–4.9x per-batch overhead (Table 2), so losing under tight latency or budget pressure is largely an expected consequence of measured slowdowns. The novel content is in the decompositions and failure modes, but the framing of rank instability as the primary discovery somewhat overstates surprise.

Some protocol parameters are chosen somewhat arbitrarily and their sensitivity is not examined: the 6σ/λ = 39.9 ms provision, the hyperbolic decay form for continuous utility (vs. exponential, which also has cognitive-science support), the single-batch buffer, and power-of-two budget spacing. Conclusions at the strictest settings (T = 50 ms, B = 1 s, ρ = 100%) drive several claims and depend on these choices.

Timing is simulated retrospectively from per-batch wall-clock measurements rather than executed on a real-time or edge testbed; given the paper's motivation from edge deployments, validation of the discrete/amortised protocols on actual constrained hardware (or at least a discussion of batch-size-dependent latency effects) is absent.

Significance is that of a benchmark/analysis contribution: no new adaptation method is proposed, and it remains an open question whether the identified design requirements (corruption-conditioned allocation, time-aware scaling, anytime performance) are simultaneously achievable—the paper stops short of showing the framework can guide method improvement in practice.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well-organised: the three temporal archetypes (discrete, continuous, amortised) are cleanly formalised, each with a scenario, protocol, and decomposable utility metric, and the notation is carefully documented (Appendix A).

The critique of Alfarra et al. (2024) is substantive and technically precise: the identified limitations (risk-free fallback evaluation, stepped penalties from the ceiling operation, forced idling) are well-argued, and Appendix B provides a fair, detailed comparison of the buffered single-model protocol against prior variants.

The utility decompositions (availability α, responsiveness κ̄, frozen accuracy ā_frozen) genuinely add explanatory value beyond a single aggregate number, e.g., diagnosing that Tent/ETA/SAR collapse to 0.1% frozen accuracy under B=1s budgets while SHOT-IM maintains ~32%, and explaining why ETA's higher served accuracy does not convert into utility.

The evaluation is broad in breadth: seven TTA methods, 15 corruptions, 16 temporal scenarios (240 evaluations), with per-corruption breakdowns and complete parameter sweeps in Appendix C, plus a stated supplementary code repository with per-batch logs, supporting reproducibility.

Limitations are discussed honestly: the paper acknowledges the episodic i.i.d. scope, the exclusion of multi-forward-pass and wrapper methods, hardware-dependence of timing, and that LAME is mismatched by design to this setting.
weaknesses: The headline finding (rank instability) is largely predictable from the latency measurements themselves: Table 2 shows gradient-based methods incur 2.4–4.9× slowdowns, so their failure under tight deadlines, latency penalties, or small budgets follows almost mechanically. The paper presents this as a novel empirical discovery, but a practitioner combining reported offline accuracies with per-batch overhead could anticipate most of the outcome.

The scope is narrow for a main-track contribution: a single dataset (ImageNet-C, severity 5 only), a single backbone (ResNet-50), a single GPU (RTX 4080), and a single seed (explicitly stated in Appendix C). Since the central claims are quantitative statements about rankings and Spearman correlations, the absence of seed variance, a second architecture (e.g., ViT), or a second dataset weakens the generality of the conclusions, which the paper itself concedes are hardware- and model-dependent.

The three metrics rest on somewhat arbitrary design choices that are not validated: the hyperbolic decay for continuous utility is justified only by loose appeal to HCI discounting literature; the continuous protocol's 'greedy user' assumption (stream synchronised to prediction emission) is a simplification that may not reflect any real deployment; and the amortised protocol's hard freeze at budget exhaustion is a modelling choice whose realism for edge devices is asserted via a stylised drone example rather than evidence.

The 'first time' framing overstates novelty. The discrete temporal evaluation already exists in Alfarra et al. (2024), whose single-model appendix variant the paper adopts nearly directly; the continuous and amortised metrics are new but incremental — hyperbolic latency discounting and compute-budget cutoffs are standard ideas re-instantiated for TTA. The contribution is a re-packaging of evaluation settings rather than a new method or a new analytical insight.

Several quantitative claims lack uncertainty quantification. Win rates (e.g., 41.2%, 58.8%), Spearman correlations, and the reported 'sharp transition' (0–7% vs 93–100% win rates) are computed from single runs; with 15 corruptions treated as independent evaluation points, correlations can be dominated by a few corruptions (e.g., brightness with 59% baseline accuracy), and no statistical test or confidence interval is provided.

Practical significance is questionable: the paper concludes that practitioners should 'validate method selection under their deployment's temporal constraints' — but Tempora's parameters (ρ, T, B, γ) must themselves be set per deployment, and the findings give no actionable selection rule beyond 'measure latency yourself'. The proposed design targets (corruption-conditioned allocation, time-aware scaling, anytime performance) are stated aspirations, not demonstrated by any method.

Some analysis is under-explained or speculative: the claim that SHOT-IM's frozen-accuracy resilience 'stems from its information maximisation objective' is explicitly a speculation, and the corruption-specific explanation (brightness 'corrects cheaply' vs Gaussian noise 'perturbs pixels independently') is asserted without any mechanistic experiment to substantiate it.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed problem: the paper convincingly argues that conventional TTA evaluation assumes unbounded processing time, and that accuracy-latency coupling determines deployment viability. This is a genuine gap relative to prior work, including Alfarra et al. (2024), whose limitations (risk-free fallback, stepped ceiling penalties, forced idling) are precisely diagnosed and addressed via a buffered single-model protocol (Appendix B is thorough and honest about design trade-offs).

The three utility metrics (discrete, continuous, amortised) are cleanly formalised, each decomposed into interpretable factors (availability α, responsiveness κ̄, adapted/frozen phases) that explain *why* rankings invert, not just that they do. The 'computational insolvency' analysis (e.g., ETA needing 149.5% served accuracy to match SAR's availability ceiling) is a particularly sharp and useful diagnostic.

Empirically substantial: 7 methods, 15 corruptions, 16 temporal scenarios (240 evaluations), with per-batch latency decomposition (Table 2) tracing rank instability to extrinsic backpropagation overhead (2.4–4.9× slowdowns). The findings — rank instability (ETA loses 41.2% of evaluations), corruption-specific Spearman correlations ranging from −0.74 to 0.21, and the striking SHOT-IM frozen-accuracy resilience under amortised budgets — are concrete, quantified, and actionable for practitioners.

Presentation quality is high: Figure 2's protocol visualisations, Figure 3's rank-instability matrix, and the notation/terminology tables (Appendix A) make a potentially confusing space easy to follow. Key terms like 'rank instability' and 'anytime performance' are well defined.

Good reproducibility posture: hyperparameters follow original implementations, supplementary code with per-batch logs is provided, and subtle implementation pitfalls (PyTorch BN running-buffer modes affecting frozen inference) are documented in detail — the kind of detail that makes results trustworthy and re-runnable.

Honest scoping and limitations discussion: episodic i.i.d. setting, single backbone/dataset, hardware-dependent timings, and the LAME mismatch are all acknowledged rather than hidden; the impact statement is appropriate.
weaknesses: External validity is narrow: all findings derive from ImageNet-C severity 5, ResNet-50, batch size 64, and a single RTX 4080. Since the metrics are defined in wall-clock terms, the specific pressure thresholds (T, ρ, B) and hence the rank-instability magnitudes are hardware-dependent; the paper claims the need to 'reconcile adaptation overhead with deployment constraints is universal,' but provides no evidence on other architectures (e.g., ViTs without BN, where several methods don't apply), datasets, or platforms.

Single-seed reporting. Accuracy under TTA methods (especially SAR with its reset mechanism, or entropy-minimisation collapse cases) can vary substantially across seeds, and headline claims like 'ETA loses in 41.2% of evaluations' or the near-zero 0.1% frozen accuracy for Tent/ETA/SAR are reported without seed variance or significance analysis. The frozen-accuracy collapse is plausibly an implementation-sensitive BN artefact (partially mitigated by their running-buffer toggle), which makes seed/implementation robustness checks important.

Several metric parameterisations are somewhat arbitrary and untested for sensitivity: the hyperbolic decay form for continuous utility, the single-batch buffer (justified by steady-state arguments but unvalidated empirically), the 6σ λ provision, and the specific T/B grids. The corruption-specific conclusions (e.g., brightness being 'cheap to correct') are plausible but asserted from post-hoc reasoning rather than verified experimentally (the paper itself admits estimating corruption difficulty without supervision is open).

Novelty is incremental relative to Alfarra et al. (2024): the discrete scenario is a refinement of their single-model variant, and the headline finding that slower gradient-based methods fare worse under time pressure is somewhat predictable. The paper's real value lies in the systematic coverage, decompositions, and reframing rather than surprising new phenomena — this is legitimate but should temper claims of revealing 'when and why rankings invert' for the first time.

Some results feel like consequences of protocol choices rather than intrinsic method properties: the amortised protocol freezes after ~20 batches for gradient-based methods, making >97% of the stream frozen inference, so the 'insolvency' conclusion at B=1s largely measures one batch-norm implementation subtlety. A fuller treatment (e.g., gradual compute scaling, alternative freeze schedules) would strengthen the amortised findings.

The Cov(a,κ) 'alignment' term in Equation 2 is algebraically trivial (a definition of covariance) and its empirical values (~0.99–1.02) suggest it carries little diagnostic content as presented; the framing slightly oversells its utility.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated framing: the paper identifies a genuine gap in TTA evaluation (temporal pressure) and grounds it in physically interpretable units (ms) rather than the model-relative proxies of Alfarra et al. (2024) and Ghunaim et al. (2023), which is a real methodological improvement.

The three utility metrics (discrete, continuous, amortised) are carefully formalised, each with a plausible deployment scenario, and are decomposable into interpretable factors (availability, responsiveness, frozen-phase accuracy). The 'computational insolvency' analysis (Table 3-5) is a genuinely insightful diagnostic that explains *why* rankings change, going beyond the prior 'whether' results.

Appendix B is exemplary: it carefully dissects Alfarra et al.'s protocol (fallback model assumptions, ceiling penalties, forced idling), quantifies the effect of each design decision (Tables 8-9), and justifies the buffered protocol. The observation that AdaBN's ranking flips from 3rd to 1st purely due to forced idling is a valuable finding for the field.

Substantial empirical scope: 750+ temporal evaluations, extension to ViT-B/16, ResNet-18, ImageNet-V2/R, CIFAR-10-C, and Raspberry Pi 5 hardware, showing rank instability is robust across architectures, datasets, and platforms. The ablation on SHOT-IM's resilience (Table 16, source running statistics) turns an observation into a mechanistic explanation.

Honest, detailed limitations discussion (single seed, default hyperparameters, episodic i.i.d. setting, excluded method families) and good reproducibility (code repository, per-batch logs, full hyperparameter specification).
weaknesses: The core phenomenon (rank instability under temporal constraints) was already established by Alfarra et al. (2024) and Ghunaim et al. (2023). The novelty lies in the broader scenario taxonomy, physical grounding, and decomposition, which is a solid but incremental advance rather than a fundamentally new insight.

The primary results rest on one benchmark configuration (ImageNet-C severity 5, ResNet-50, single seed, single GPU), with generality deferred to the appendix. Given that protocol design choices themselves shift rankings substantially (e.g., Table 8's AdaBN flip), the sensitivity of conclusions to protocol and seed choices deserves more direct statistical treatment.

Metric design choices, while individually justified (hyperbolic decay from HCI literature, 6-sigma latency provision, budget grid), involve enough free parameters that an unfavourable design could plausibly alter some conclusions; the paper acknowledges this but does not fully quantify it.

The dramatic frozen-accuracy collapse under amortised evaluation (0.1% for most gradient-based methods) appears partly implementation-contingent (the paper's own SHOT-IM*/ETA* ablation shows preserving source statistics reverses it), so the 'harmful adaptation' failure mode is as much a property of current implementations as of the paradigm.
The paper is purely diagnostic: it proposes no method satisfying the three identified properties, leaving the practical impact contingent on future work adopting the framework.

strengths: The problem framing is well-motivated: conventional TTA evaluation assumes unbounded processing time, and the paper makes a convincing case that temporal pressure determines system viability in latency-sensitive deployments.

The protocol revisions of Alfarra et al. (2024) are careful and well-argued; the buffered single-model discrete protocol (Appendix B), the identification of forced idling and stepped penalties, and the empirical demonstration of how buffering changes AdaBN's ranking (Table 8) are genuinely useful contributions to evaluation methodology.

The decomposable utility metrics are a nice diagnostic idea: separating availability, responsiveness, and frozen-phase accuracy yields concrete failure modes (availability collapse, accuracy erosion, harmful adaptation) and the SHOT-IM source-statistics ablation (Table 16) is a particularly compelling causal analysis.

The evaluation is extensive: multiple parameter sweeps, per-corruption analysis, rank-correlation tables, and an extended suite (ViT-B/16, ImageNet-V2/R, CIFAR-10-C, Raspberry Pi 5) that supports the generality claims.

The limitations section is unusually honest, explicitly discussing hyperparameter confounds, method-evaluation mismatch (LAME), and the hardware-dependence of conclusions; code and per-batch logs are promised, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central finding has limited surprise value. That gradient-based methods with 2.4-4.9x overhead (Table 2) lose to cheap methods under deadline pressure is close to a foregone conclusion once per-method latency is measured; 'rank instability' largely reduces to the statement that accuracy and latency trade off, and the three metrics are simple products/weighted combinations that formalise this trade-off rather than reveal new structure.

Incremental originality relative to Alfarra et al. (2024) and Ghunaim et al. (2023): the core discrete scenario is inherited, and the main advances are a physical-unit reparameterisation, a buffering fix, and two additional penalty functions. The hyperbolic decay and HCI anchoring of T are plausible but unvalidated, and the 6-sigma lambda provision is an arbitrary-but-consequential modelling choice.

The headline counts inflate the empirical scope: '750+ evaluations' counts every (corruption, parameter) cell of a sweep as a separate evaluation; the underlying design is one benchmark, one backbone, one GPU, one seed for the main results. The generality claims rest entirely on appendix material.

No statistical treatment: results are from a single seed with default hyperparameters, and the authors themselves concede hyperparameter influence on rankings is an unresolved epistemic concern. Given that several conclusions (e.g., CMF's 12.1% win rate, method-pair reversals) depend on ranking stability, this is a material weakness.

The claimed 'three necessary properties for deployable adaptation' (Section 4.3) are design desiderata derived from the failures observed, not validated principles; no method is designed or modified to test whether satisfying them actually improves temporal utility, which limits the prescriptive force of the conclusions.

The amortised results (0.1% frozen accuracy for most methods) appear substantially driven by a BN running-statistics implementation artefact; the ablation is welcome, but it suggests some headline failure modes reflect implementation conventions rather than intrinsic method properties.

strengths: The problem is well-motivated and clearly framed: conventional TTA evaluation implicitly assumes unbounded processing time, and the paper operationalises 'accuracy-latency joint viability' through three deployment-grounded scenarios (hard deadlines, latency-sensitive interactivity, budget-constrained overhead).

The framework is a genuine advance over Alfarra et al. (2024): grounding constraints in physical units (ms) rather than model-relative proxies, removing the fallback-model safety net, introducing a buffered single-model protocol that avoids forced idling and stepped ceiling penalties, and adding two new scenario archetypes (continuous and amortised). The appendix treatment of the protocol revision (Appendix B, Tables 8-9) is unusually careful, including an honest quantification of how the buffer changes prior conclusions.

The metrics are decomposable and diagnostic rather than purely aggregative: availability vs. served accuracy (discrete), responsiveness and accuracy-responsiveness covariance (continuous), and adapted/frozen phase accuracies (amortised). This yields concrete, mechanistic findings, e.g., the frozen-accuracy collapse to 0.1% for most gradient-based methods under amortised evaluation, and the SHOT-IM outlier traced to retained source running statistics, confirmed by ablation (Table 16).

Empirical coverage is extensive: 11 methods, 240 evaluations per method on ImageNet-C/ResNet-50, plus ViT-B/16, ImageNet-V2/R, CIFAR-10-C, and Raspberry Pi 5 hardware in the appendix, with rank instability persisting throughout. The appendix reports complete parameter sweeps, per-corruption winners, Spearman correlations, and deficit profiles, making the claims verifiable from the manuscript itself.

The derived design implications (corruption-conditioned compute allocation, time-aware scaling, anytime performance) follow logically from the observed failure modes and give the paper actionable value beyond negative findings.

Limitations are discussed candidly (single seed, default hyperparameters, episodic i.i.d. setup, excluded method families, simulation rather than real-time testbed), and the impact statement is appropriate. The code and per-batch logs are promised, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Originality is moderate: the core discrete scenario is a revision of Alfarra et al. (2024)'s protocol, and the continuous and amortised metrics, while sensibly designed, are relatively simple functional forms (hyperbolic decay, budget cutoff with freeze). The paper's value rests more on thoroughness and diagnosis than on novel methodology.

All primary results are on a single seed, single GPU, and a single primary backbone; the generalisation suite (ViT-B/16, other datasets, CPU hardware) is confined to the appendix. Seed/hyperparameter sensitivity is acknowledged but not measured for the headline rank-instability claims.

The evaluations simulate asynchronous streams retrospectively via a discrete-event simulation rather than running on a real-time testbed; wall-clock measurement noise, system jitter, and competing processes are not modelled, which matters for a paper whose central claim concerns physically grounded deployment realism.

Some metric design choices appear ad hoc and are not ablated: the hyperbolic decay form (vs. alternatives such as exponential or threshold-cliff penalties), the single-batch buffer size, and the specific grids for T, B, and rho. Conclusions could be sensitive to these choices, particularly the buffer, which materially reshuffles rankings (e.g., AdaBN moves from rank 3 to 1).

The headline count of '750+ temporal evaluations' is inflated by counting parameter-sweep cells as independent evaluations; the number of independent experimental conditions (methods x scenarios x datasets x hardware) is considerably smaller.

The central empirical finding - that slow, gradient-heavy methods fare worse under tight temporal constraints - is somewhat anticipated by prior work (Alfarra et al. 2024; Ghunaim et al. 2023); the contribution is in breadth, decomposition, and physical interpretability rather than a surprising discovery.
The code link appears incomplete in the manuscript (the 'Code:' field is blank on page 1), which weakens the reproducibility claim as submitted.
